subject: Biology
description: Biome types, food chain, ecological pyramids, ecosystem dynamics

questions.stem: A FOOD CHAIN typically begins with:
questions.explanation: FOOD CHAIN starts with PRODUCERS (autotrophs — green plants, algae, cyanobacteria) — they make food by photosynthesis. Next: PRIMARY CONSUMERS (herbivores) → SECONDARY CONSUMERS (small carnivores) → TERTIARY (top predators). DECOMPOSERS (bacteria, fungi) break down dead matter at all levels, recycling nutrients. ENERGY FLOW = unidirectional (one-way: plants → animals → decomposers). ~10% energy passes to next trophic level (Lindeman's 10% rule). Hence food chains rarely exceed 4-5 levels.

questions.stem: The TROPICAL RAINFOREST biome is characterised by:

options.option_text: Hot dry summers, with little rainfall
Permanent ice cover over the soil

questions.explanation: TROPICAL RAINFORESTS — found near equator (Amazon, Congo, Indonesia, NE India, Western Ghats). Climate: high temperature (~25-30°C year-round), high humidity, RAINFALL >2000 mm/year (often >3000 mm). HIGHEST BIODIVERSITY of any biome (~50% of world's species in ~5% of land). Layers: emergent, canopy, understory, forest floor. India: Western Ghats, NE states, Andaman + Nicobar. Threats: deforestation, agriculture, mining. Distractor 1 = tundra. Distractor 3 = desert. Distractor 4 = polar / glacier.

questions.stem: Plants of TROPICAL DESERT biome (cactus, agave) often show which adaptations?

options.option_text: Broad leaves to capture more sunlight

questions.explanation: DESERT plants (XEROPHYTES) adaptations to extreme dry, high heat: (1) reduced leaves → SPINES (cactus); (2) thick fleshy STEMS for water storage (cactus is mostly water); (3) waxy cuticle to reduce evaporation; (4) deep / wide roots; (5) CAM photosynthesis (open stomata at NIGHT — close in day to save water; e.g., agave, pineapple). Indian deserts: Thar (hot), Ladakh (cold). Major desert biomes: Sahara, Gobi, Kalahari, Atacama (driest), Australian Outback.

questions.stem: An ECOLOGICAL PYRAMID OF NUMBERS in a typical grassland (grass → grasshoppers → birds → snakes) is:
questions.explanation: PYRAMIDS OF NUMBERS — show count of organisms at each trophic level. Most ecosystems: UPRIGHT (many producers → fewer consumers). Exceptions: TREE → caterpillars → birds (one tree supports thousands of caterpillars → INVERTED at producer level). Parasitic chains: host → parasites → hyperparasites (inverted overall). PYRAMIDS OF BIOMASS — usually upright too; aquatic ecosystems often INVERTED (tiny phytoplankton turn over fast; small biomass at any moment but high productivity). PYRAMIDS OF ENERGY — ALWAYS UPRIGHT (10% rule).

questions.stem: An organism (animal/plant) that is found ONLY in a particular geographical area is called:
questions.explanation: ENDEMIC = restricted to a particular geographical area; found nowhere else naturally. India is rich in endemics — esp. Western Ghats + NE India + Andaman-Nicobar. Examples: LION-TAILED MACAQUE (Western Ghats); NILGIRI TAHR (Nilgiris); ASIATIC LION (Gir, only place in world); SANGAI deer (Loktak Lake, Manipur); Nicobar megapode (Nicobar). Distractor 1 'cosmopolitan' = found worldwide (housefly, dandelion). Distractor 3 'migratory' = seasonal travellers. Distractor 4 'invasive' = non-native, harmful (water hyacinth, lantana).

options.option_text: Increase in biomass over generations of organisms
Concentration of toxins rising up the food chain
Genetic mutations spreading in a population pool

questions.explanation: BIOMAGNIFICATION (or biological magnification) — non-degradable toxins (DDT, mercury, lead, PCBs) accumulate at HIGHER concentrations as we move UP the food chain. e.g., DDT in water (~0.003 ppm) → in plankton (~0.04) → small fish (~0.5) → large fish (~2) → bird of prey (~25 ppm). Result: TOP PREDATORS most affected. Famous case: BALD EAGLE in 1960s — DDT caused thinning of eggshells, near-extinction. Rachel Carson's 'Silent Spring' (1962) sparked environmental movement. DDT banned in many countries (India still uses for malaria control under WHO guidelines). MERCURY in fish (Minamata Bay disaster).

questions.stem: SUNDARBANS, India's famous mangrove forest, is mainly characterised by:

options.option_text: Tall deciduous trees of the plains

questions.explanation: SUNDARBANS (West Bengal + Bangladesh) — world's largest MANGROVE forest, in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta. Mangroves = trees adapted to TIDAL salty water. Key adaptations: (1) PROP / STILT roots (hold soft mud); (2) PNEUMATOPHORES — aerial roots that breathe (snorkel-like); (3) salt-excreting leaves; (4) viviparous seeds (germinate on parent tree). Famous tree: SUNDRI (Heritiera fomes — gives name to Sundarbans). Home to ROYAL BENGAL TIGER (Panthera tigris tigris), saltwater crocodiles. UNESCO WHS (1987 — Sundarbans NP, India side; 1997 — Bangladesh side).
